items.summary: Certain taxonomic debates resurface time and again.

items.title: Scientists find the whole grain “sweet spot” for better heart health
items.summary: Eating four to six servings of whole grains a day may deliver meaningful benefits for heart health, according to a large review of 87 clinical trials. Researchers found improvements in body weight, waist size, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, triglycerides, and some markers of inflammation.

items.title: Nearly 50 'ghost galaxies' emerge around three hosts, challenging dwarf galaxy counts
items.summary: Dwarf galaxies—with a mass equal to about a billion suns, but often considerably less—are the most abundant in the universe. However, because of their low luminosity, they are very difficult to detect. They have mostly been discovered in the vicinity of the Milky Way, in what is called the Local Gro

items.title: The hidden cost of pressure to be a perfect parent
items.summary: The pressure to be the perfect parent can be overwhelming, but social media and perceived world threats are causing some to become overprotective parents, negatively affecting young people.

items.title: Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
items.summary: Scientists reconstructed videos from the brain activity of mice, producing 10-second clips based only on signals from neurons in the visual cortex. The breakthrough could help reveal how the brain reshapes what we see before it becomes our perception of reality.

items.title: A third of Americans cannot name the three branches of government
items.summary: Over a third of U.S. adults (35%) cannot name all three branches of the government, and under half can name four of the five rights protected by the First Amendment, according to the 2026 Annenberg Constitution Day Civics Survey from the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pen

items.title: Webb measures extreme gas outflows from distant 'dead' galaxies
items.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have measured the most powerful gas outflow ever recorded from a "dead" galaxy outside our cosmic neighborhood and found that even outflows this extreme may not be enough to permanently shut down star formation.

items.title: Thousands of the most vulnerable children and young people missing out on mental health support
items.summary: Some of the most vulnerable children and young people are failing to access mental health support despite having much higher levels of need, according to new research from the University of Cambridge.

items.title: Sibling interactions are an untapped resource for early engineering education, study suggests
items.summary: While parents' roles in a child's education are well studied, new research examines the role siblings play in collaborating on educational projects. Researchers found that siblings often develop a few key roles in these working relationships.

items.title: Venus may have swallowed its own moon
items.summary: Venus may have once had a moon, but new research suggests the planet’s incredibly slow rotation could have doomed it. items.title: New breeding approach targets crop rotations, not yield alone
items.summary: Breeding crops for farming systems rather than yield alone could exploit untapped genetic potential and help farmers cut fertilizer bills.

items.title: Fewer than half of Americans expect free and fair midterms
items.summary: Americans are heading into the 2026 midterm elections with widespread uncertainty about the integrity of the vote, according to a new national survey from the University of California San Diego.

items.title: Irrigation’s climate benefit could equal 363 years of its own emissions
items.summary: U.S. irrigation produces some greenhouse gas emissions, but new research suggests it prevents vastly more by allowing farmers to grow more food on less land. Without irrigation, replacing lost crop yields could require converting natural ecosystems into farmland, releasing an estimated 6.86 gigatons

items.title: Australia's ancient rainfall patterns more complex than previously believed
items.summary: "Sediment and fossil records are a major pillar of our understanding of how the climate works—but climate scientists have gotten something wrong about Australia's ice age," says Dr. Alex F. Wall, lead author of a new research paper published in Quaternary Science Reviews.

items.title: 'Invisible work' of AI falls disproportionately to middle managers, women
items.summary: It's a common refrain that AI is changing how we work, but new research conducted by the Notre Dame-IBM Tech Ethics Lab, housed in the Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, shows that AI is creating new forms of work and reconfiguring employees' lived experience of work itself.

items.title: Weeping whales: Stillborn humpback whale grieving documented
items.summary: Humpback whale mothers may experience grief when their calves die, a rare research observation led by Griffith University and Sea World Foundation has found.

items.title: Scientists “truly astonished” by discovery that challenges Earth’s origin story
items.summary: A new study suggests Earth formed almost entirely from material in the inner Solar System, challenging the idea that water-rich material from beyond Jupiter played a major role. If correct, Earth’s water may have been present much closer to the young Sun than scientists previously thought.

items.title: Nine in 10 UK gambling websites breach data privacy law, study finds
items.summary: Nearly nine in 10 (86%) UK-licensed online gambling websites are operating in breach of the General Data Protection Regulation, according to new research from the Gambling Research, Education and Treatment (GREAT) Center at Swansea University published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior Repo

items.title: First-of-its-kind preventive phage therapy provides promising results against Salmonella
items.summary: The mammalian gut microbiome teems with a delicate balance of bacteria and the viruses that keep them in check, called bacteriophages, or phages. Each bacterial species usually has its own set of phage partners.

items.title: New simulations link unusual particle diffusion to yielding in soft jammed matter
items.summary: Soft materials such as colloidal suspensions, emulsions, foams and gels often display complex and unusual behaviors compared with ordinary solids or liquids. items.title: 'Born-again' star offers rare chance to watch stellar evolution in real time
items.summary: Astronomers have confirmed that one of the fastest-changing stars ever observed has entered a new stage of its evolution, offering a rare opportunity to watch a star's life unfold on human timescales.

items.title: Speeding glaciers drive half a century of polar ice loss
items.summary: The longest satellite record ever assembled shows that Greenland and Antarctica have lost 11.3 trillion metric tons of ice since the 1970s, raising global sea level by more than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches)—and that most of the loss has come from glaciers flowing faster into the ocean, not from meltin

items.title: The local costs of remote sensing: Examining the ethics of laser scanning in tropical forests
items.summary: Laser scanning, often referred to as lidar, has rapidly transformed how tropical forest regions are studied, monitored and understood across academic disciplines. The technology enables researchers to peer through dense forest canopies, rapidly providing high-resolution scans of the landscape below.

items.title: Wildfires push endangered Sumatran elephants to brink: Indonesian NGO
items.summary: Critically endangered Sumatran elephants are being pushed closer to the brink as wildfires raze vast swaths of their habitat on the western island of Sumatra, Indonesian conservation group Geopix told AFP on Wednesday.

items.title: SpaceX prepares for first orbital flight of Starship rocket
items.summary: SpaceX announced Tuesday that it was planning to send its flagship rocket, Starship, into orbit, a key step in its project to one day reach the moon or Mars.

items.title: US acknowledges for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space
items.summary: The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, a remarkable revelation after previous warnings about countries such as Russia possibly weaponizing a global frontier long agreed in treaties to be used for only peaceful purposes.

items.title: Well-preserved tooth from Pacific mastodon found in a creek in San Francisco Bay Area
items.summary: Brigid Lynch was working along a wooded creek in a mountainous part of the San Francisco Bay Area when something that didn't look like the rocks she'd been studying caught her eye. It turned out to be the fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon.

items.title: A world 20 light-years away reveals surprisingly organized, Jupiter-like weather
items.summary: Scientists from Trinity College Dublin have developed a way to unravel changing weather patterns on distant worlds. items.title: Study finds violence affects millions across US with links to health, economic hardship
items.summary: A new national study reveals the widespread reach of violence across the United States, finding that more than half of U.S. adults have experienced physical violence and nearly half have experienced sexual violence in their lifetimes. The U.S. National Study on Violence Experiences Across the Lifesp

items.title: Chimpanzees give youngsters the tools to learn tricky techniques
items.summary: Two-thirds of a century after Jane Goodall observed "David Greybeard" break off a twig to fashion a fishing rod for termites, researchers following in her footsteps have found that adult chimpanzees in Senegal literally hand youngsters the tools for learning.

items.title: James Webb reveals Chariklo’s mysterious rings are changing faster than expected
items.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed surprising changes in the rings around Chariklo, a small object orbiting between Saturn and Uranus. items.summary: According to research by the IfM Bonn, strengthening research collaboration between universities and businesses requires regional technology transfer networks in which technology transfer offices at universities and research institutions, as well as chambers of commerce and industry, trade associati

items.title: Ultra-processed foods linked to hidden muscle fat that may threaten your knees
items.summary: Eating more ultra-processed foods was linked to greater fat buildup inside thigh muscles, according to MRI scans of 615 adults at risk for knee osteoarthritis. Surprisingly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for calorie intake, physical activity, and other factors. Fatty chan

items.title: How high turnover rates in Tanzania's agro-dealer sector affect farmer fertilizer adoption
items.summary: Smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa adopt agricultural inputs, including fertilizer, at low rates, contributing to low agricultural productivity. items.title: Scientists find a hidden retinal defense against vision loss
items.summary: A naturally occurring molecule called erucamide may help the retina fight back against diseases that cause progressive vision loss. Restoring the molecule activated protective immune responses that helped stabilize retinal tissue and slow aspects of degeneration in preclinical models.

items.title: A new mechanism for reading extra-long genes in neurons
items.summary: Neurons in humans and other mammals express many exceptionally long genes, ranging from more than 100 kbp to more than 2 Mbp, that are important for forming synapses and neural circuits. items.title: Study explores new photonics advance: Topology imprinting in nonlinear metasurfaces
items.summary: Light is traditionally described by properties such as wavelength, amplitude, phase and polarization. Advances in optics have shown that light can also be shaped into complex spatial patterns known as structured light, enabling new ways to carry information and interact with matter for applications

items.title: Scientists reversed biological age in older adults in just 4 weeks
items.summary: Older adults who changed the balance of fat, carbohydrates, and animal protein in their diets showed signs of reduced biological age after just four weeks. The strongest result appeared in participants eating an omnivorous, lower-fat, higher-carbohydrate diet.

items.title: Four in 10 young people don't see 'buy now, pay later' as debt
items.summary: The way a product is labeled can change how consumers think about it. "No added sugar" or "99% fat-free" can make food sound healthier than it really is.

items.title: Greyhound racing just turned 100, and says its dogs are fine. But are they?
items.summary: This year, greyhound racing in Britain turns 100 years old. The first race took place on July 24, 1926, in Manchester, where six dogs chased a mechanical hare around a track.

items.title: NASA Ames Stars of the Month: September 2026
items.summary: The NASA Ames Science Directorate recognizes the outstanding contributions of (pictured left to right) Steve Ormsby, Aphrodite Kostakis, Alejando Borlaff, Sarah Nickerson, Martina Caussi, Keiko Nomura, and Stephen Broccardo. items.title: High-resolution weather data could pinpoint neighborhoods facing greatest heat stress
items.summary: Heat stress is a leading cause of weather-related deaths and can be especially dangerous in cities, where phenomena like urban heat islands drive temperatures higher than in surrounding rural areas. Now, a new dataset developed by the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric

items.title: New species of 240-million-year-old prehistoric animal could reshape dinosaur origins timeline
items.summary: A new prehistoric animal species from Tanzania dating to around 240 million years ago, during the Triassic period, has been described by an international team of researchers. items.summary: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) can be harmful to the environment in large amounts but can be used in the production of fuels and other useful chemicals. Doing so isn't easy, though.
